A Closer Look At WDB coco's Earnings

In high finance, the key ratio used to measure how well a company converts reported profits into free cash flow (FCF) is the accrual ratio (from cashflow). In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. While having an accrual ratio above zero is of little concern, we do think it's worth noting when a company has a relatively high accrual ratio. That's because some academic studies have suggested that high accruals ratios tend to lead to lower profit or less profit growth.

For the year to September 2026, WDB coco had an accrual ratio of -0.26. Therefore, its statutory earnings were very significantly less than its free cashflow. Indeed, in the last twelve months it reported free cash flow of JP¥938m, well over the JP¥732.0m it reported in profit. Examining Cashflow Against Eiwa's Earnings

As finance nerds would already know, the accrual ratio from cashflow is a key measure for assessing how well a company's free cash flow (FCF) matches its profit. In plain english, this ratio subtracts FCF from net profit, and divides that number by the company's average operating assets over that period. The ratio shows us how much a company's profit exceeds its FCF.

As a result, a negative accrual ratio is a positive for the company, and a positive accrual ratio is a negative. While it's not a problem to have a positive accrual ratio, indicating a certain level of non-cash profits, a high accrual ratio is arguably a bad thing, because it indicates paper profits are not matched by cash flow. Notably, there is some academic evidence that suggests that a high accrual ratio is a bad sign for near-term profits, generally speaking.

Eiwa has an accrual ratio of 0.31 for the year to September 2026. Therefore, we know that it's free cashflow was significantly lower than its statutory profit, raising questions about how useful that profit figure really is. Over the last year it actually had negative free cash flow of JP¥1.8b, in contrast to the aforementioned profit of JP¥2.24b. Coming off the back of negative free cash flow last year, we imagine some shareholders might wonder if its cash burn of JP¥1.8b, this year, indicates high risk.

Our Take On Eiwa's Profit Performance

Eiwa's accrual ratio for the last twelve months signifies cash conversion is less than ideal, which is a negative when it comes to our view of its earnings. Because of this, we think that it may be that Eiwa's statutory profits are better than its underlying earnings power. Nonetheless, it's still worth noting that its earnings per share have grown at 36% over the last three years. For example, although Amazon.com made losses for many years after listing, if you had bought and held the shares since 1999, you would have made a fortune. Nonetheless, only a fool would ignore the risk that a loss making company burns through its cash too quickly.

Given this risk, we thought we'd take a look at whether Japan Tissue Engineering (TSE:7774) shareholders should be worried about its cash burn. Does Japan Tissue Engineering Have A Long Cash Runway?

A company's cash runway is the amount of time it would take to burn through its cash reserves at its current cash burn rate. When Japan Tissue Engineering last reported its September 2026 balance sheet in October 2026, it had zero debt and cash worth JP¥3.3b. Importantly, its cash burn was JP¥332m over the trailing twelve months. That means it had a cash runway of very many years as of September 2026. Japan Tissue Engineering actually ramped up its cash burn by a whopping 98% in the last year, which shows it is boosting investment in the business. While that certainly gives us pause for thought, we take a lot of comfort in the strong annual revenue growth of 72%. How Hard Would It Be For Japan Tissue Engineering To Raise More Cash For Growth?

We are certainly impressed with the progress Japan Tissue Engineering has made over the last year, but it is also worth considering how costly it would be if it wanted to raise more cash to fund faster growth. Issuing new shares, or taking on debt, are the most common ways for a listed company to raise more money for its business. Commonly, a business will sell new shares in itself to raise cash and drive growth. We can compare a company's cash burn to its market capitalisation to get a sense for how many new shares a company would have to issue to fund one year's operations.

Since it has a market capitalisation of JP¥27b, Japan Tissue Engineering's JP¥332m in cash burn equates to about 1.3% of its market value. That means it could easily issue a few shares to fund more growth, and might well be in a position to borrow cheaply.

Is Japan Tissue Engineering's Cash Burn A Worry?

It may already be apparent to you that we're relatively comfortable with the way Japan Tissue Engineering is burning through its cash. In particular, we think its revenue growth stands out as evidence that the company is well on top of its spending. While we must concede that its increasing cash burn is a bit worrying, the other factors mentioned in this article provide great comfort when it comes to the cash burn.
